meta.title: Spanish Regional Vocabulary — Declarative Schema
meta.note: LANG-01 established this file's schema only (zero entries). LANG-02 (terminology research phase) populated the entries below with researched Spanish vocabulary mapped onto existing canonical ontology entity_ids. See reports/spanish-vocabulary-research-lang02.json for methodology, coverage, and flagged unresolved terminology (notably a pre-existing bare-slug identity collision between grape-catalog.json/wine-style-catalog.json and between wine-style-catalog.json/wine-region-catalog.json, which the current schema cannot represent as distinct entities).

entry_contract.description: One vocabulary entry maps ONE existing, language-neutral ontology entity_id to ONE Spanish regional profile's preferred term and known aliases. An entry never creates a new entity, never redefines entity identity, and never exists for a language other than Spanish (English needs no vocabulary layer — see docs/LANGUAGE_GOVERNANCE.md §7).

entity_id.description: MUST reference an existing, unmodified canonical entity id from an existing data/*-catalog.json (e.g. food.fruit.tropical-fruits.avocado). A vocabulary entry MUST NOT be the source of a new entity id — it is a projection onto an id that already exists in the language-neutral ontology.

language.description: MUST be "es". This schema exists for Spanish regional vocabulary specifically; a future additional language would get its own schema file and registry entry, not a value in this enum.

region.description: MUST be one of the five registered regional profile ids in lib/language-config.js. "ca" denotes the Central America vocabulary profile — never Canada, never an ISO 3166 code, never a distinct publication.

preferred.description: The term that SHOULD normally appear in generated Spanish copy for this entity, in this regional profile. Exactly one preferred term per (entity_id, language, region) triple — never a list.

aliases.description: Recognized alternative terms for the same entity in this regional profile. Aliases exist for recognition, search terminology, vocabulary resolution, entity matching, and future localization/search features — they are NOT candidates for automatic promotion into rendered copy. An alias array MAY be empty; it is never required to be non-empty.

notes.description: Optional terminology note — e.g. why a regional term was chosen, a register/formality distinction, a disambiguation from a false-friend term. Editorial metadata only; never rendered directly as-is without review.

entry_contract.uniqueness_contract: At most one entry per (entity_id, language, region) triple. Multiple entries for the same entity_id across different regions are expected and normal — that is the whole point of the regional layer.
entry_contract.fallback_contract: A missing entry for (entity_id, es, <region>) is not an error — see docs/LANGUAGE_GOVERNANCE.md §10. Resolution falls back to (entity_id, es, neutral), then to the entity's approved language-neutral fallback (its existing English display_name, never a fabricated Spanish term). Most entities are expected to need zero regional overrides and rely entirely on this fallback.

example_shape_for_illustration_only.note: Illustrates the intended shape. This is NOT a populated entry and MUST NOT be treated as real vocabulary data — see meta.status above.

"Syrah" is the standard term in Spanish-language wine writing; "Shiraz" (the Australian/South African usage) is kept as an alias since it appears on imported labels.

Garnacha is a Spanish grape originating in Aragón; the Spanish name is the primary term in Spanish-language wine writing, with the French "Grenache" as a recognized alias for imported/international bottlings.

"Champán" is the standard Spanish-language adaptation; the French spelling "Champagne" is a common alias, especially on imported labeling. "Oporto" is the established Spanish name for Port wine, after the Portuguese city. "Port" appears as an alias from English-language labeling.

"Jerez" is the Spanish name (the wine's own denomination of origin, Jerez de la Frontera); "Sherry" is the English-market name and a common alias.
"Moscato" (Italian) is used for the Italian style specifically; "Moscatel" is the Spanish-language grape/wine name generally and is kept as alias since both appear on Spanish-language retail.
"Vacuno" is the standard everyday term for beef in Chile; "res" is understood but less commonly used as the primary category label.
"Puerco" is widely used colloquially in Mexico alongside "cerdo"; both are correct, "puerco" is the more common spoken form.
In Spain "soja" is the standard form; "soya" is the standard form across most of Latin America (kept as the neutral term for broader reach).

In Spain, 'boquerón' properly names the fresh anchovy and 'anchoa' the cured/salted product; both are offered as recognized alternates here since the catalog entity does not distinguish preparation state.
Kept as a descriptive loanword rather than 'Requesón', which properly names a distinct whey cheese, not cottage cheese.
"Aguacate" is understood everywhere and is the standard term in Mexico, Central America, and Spain; Chile's distinct everyday term is encoded below.
"Palta" is the standard everyday term across the Southern Cone (Chile, Argentina, Peru, Uruguay, Bolivia).

"Toronja" is standard in Mexico, Central America, and much of Latin America; "pomelo" is standard in Spain and the Southern Cone.

"Lima" is the technically precise neutral term; in much everyday Latin American Spanish "limón" is used for both lemon and lime, kept as alias for recognition, not promoted to preferred since it would collide with the lemon entity's own preferred term.

"Papaya" is broadly understood everywhere; "lechosa" (Venezuela/Dominican Republic) and "fruta bomba" (Cuba) are notable aliases from other Spanish-speaking regions outside the 5 approved profiles, kept for recognition only.

"Maicena" (originally a brand name) has become the everyday generic term across most of the Spanish-speaking world, similar to "Kleenex" in English; "fécula/almidón de maíz" is the formal/technical term, kept as alias.

"Nixtamal"/"maíz pozolero" is standard in Mexico; "mote" is the standard term in the Southern Cone. No single neutral term is truly universal here, so the Mexico-oriented "maíz pozolero" is kept neutral (broadest recognizability) with both regional terms as aliases rather than fabricating a separate cl entry not clearly evidenced for THIS specific processed form.

entries.notes: Standard Spanish term; not 'salsa de manzana', which reads as a savory sauce rather than the smooth cooked-apple preparation.
Qualified as 'rojo' to distinguish from arándano azul (blueberry).
'Mahonesa' is the historically original Spanish spelling (from Mahón, Menorca) and remains a recognized formal alias in Spain, though 'Mayonesa' is now the standard everyday term everywhere.
Established Spanish culinary term, not a literal translation of 'orange blossom'.
'Salsa Inglesa' is the established everyday term across the Spanish-speaking world, not a literal translation.
"Hongos" is the broadest, most universally understood neutral term across the Spanish-speaking world.
In Spain, "setas" is the standard culinary term for edible mushrooms; "hongos" reads as more technical/mycological and can carry a mold connotation. Reversed preference from neutral, not a new fact.
Established Spanish common name for Pleurotus eryngii, not a literal translation of 'king oyster'.
The everyday market/menu term in Spain for Boletus edulis.
